steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Let your younger son move a passenger while your older son updates the stored number. Use totals from zero to three. Pause to compare the card with the toys, then deliberately leave an old card in place and repair the mismatch together.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Show the final passenger count and explain how the label helped you know what the number meant.

personalPrompt: Where do you keep a changing number, such as a count of jobs left? Explain why its label matters.
careNote: Use large toddler-safe figures and large number cards without clips. Keep the bus a drawing; do not use a box for children to climb into or ride.

title: Sort it another way
subtitle: Find more than one sensible way to make groups.
takeaway: The same collection can be grouped differently depending on the rule we choose.
parentPrimer: Choose a few large familiar objects with overlapping features, such as soft toys and sturdy books in different colours. Sort by one visible feature, then another. An object can belong in different groups under different rules. Explain your reasoning and accept a child's alternative rule when they can show it.
materials: A small collection of large toddler-safe toys and sturdy books

toddler.action: Choose between two objects or place one beside another that feels similar.
toddler.question: Which one could go with this?

older.action: Choose a sorting rule, explain a placement, then regroup the collection using a different feature.
older.question: Could this object belong somewhere else if our rule changed?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Put a soft toy next to a sturdy book and notice one difference.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Sort a few objects by whether they are soft, and explain the rule aloud.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Let your younger son choose objects while your older son labels two groups with pictures. Try another rule, such as objects with wheels and objects without. Discuss an awkward example rather than forcing it into a group, and invent a rule together.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Choose one object that moved groups and remember why its place changed.

personalPrompt: When do you organise the same things in different ways? Share an example from books, tools, or files.
careNote: Use only large intact familiar objects without batteries accessible to children or detachable pieces. Keep the collection small and place it on a stable low surface.

title: Which question helps?
subtitle: Choose a question that separates two possibilities.
takeaway: A useful question can help us tell possible explanations apart.
parentPrimer: Choose three visible large toys and privately select one in your mind. Children ask yes-or-no questions about observable features. A question like does it have wheels can narrow the choices; a feature all three share may not. Keep the answer consistent and allow pointing or direct guesses.
materials: Three large familiar toys with different visible features

toddler.action: Point to a possible toy or show a feature you name together.
toddler.question: Which toy has wheels?

older.action: Ask a question, remove choices that do not fit the answer, and explain which question helped.
older.question: Would that question tell these two toys apart?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Line up three toys and say that you are thinking of one of them.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Model a question about a visible feature and show how its answer changes the possibilities.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Let your younger son point to candidates while your older son asks questions. Discuss which toys still fit after each answer. Reveal the toy whenever wanted, then swap who chooses and try a new question.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Remember one question that helped and another that left several possibilities open.

personalPrompt: When did asking a more specific question help you understand a problem? Share a simple example.
careNote: Use large toddler-safe toys and keep them visible. No blindfolds or hiding objects in mouths, clothes, or places children would need to climb to reach.

title: A plan for a toy visitor
subtitle: Make a choice, then see what a new detail changes.
takeaway: A new requirement can change which option works best for a goal.
parentPrimer: Imagine a toy visitor needs a place to rest. Compare a broad cushion and a small folded towel using a chosen goal, such as room for two toys. Add a new pretend detail and reconsider. Separate a preference from an observation: I like blue and both toys fit are different reasons.

toddler.action: Choose a resting place for a toy and help check whether another toy fits beside it.
toddler.question: Where could our visitor rest?

older.action: Compare two choices against a goal, then revise the plan when a second visitor arrives.
older.question: Does our first choice still work with this new detail?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Introduce a pretend visitor looking for a resting place.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Compare the cushion and towel. Name a preference and an observable reason for choosing each.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Let your younger son settle the toy while your older son explains a choice. Bring a second toy visitor and check the plan again. Try a new pretend need, such as keeping both toys side by side, and discuss whether the choice changes.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Thank each other for a helpful idea and name the detail that mattered most to the final plan.

personalPrompt: When have changed plans helped you respond to someone else's needs? Share an ordinary example.
careNote: Use cushions and towels as toy resting places on the floor. Keep children's faces clear and avoid wrapping anyone in fabric or piling cushions high.

title: A roof for a toy
subtitle: Design a tiny shelter with room underneath.
takeaway: A design can be checked against what it needs to do, then improved.
parentPrimer: Give a large toy a simple design brief: a roof that stays up and leaves room for the toy underneath. Use low stacks of large blocks and a sheet of card. Test by gently placing the toy, not by adding heavy loads. A collapsed roof is information about the design.
materials: A large sheet of card with smooth edges

toddler.action: Choose the toy and help place a large support block with you.
toddler.question: Can our toy fit underneath?

older.action: Plan the roof's supports, check the space underneath, and change one part after a test.
older.question: What could make the roof steadier without blocking the doorway?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: A toy needs a little pretend shelter. Ask what its roof should do.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Make a very low roof with two supports and check whether the toy fits.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can move the toy in and out while your older son adjusts the supports. Try wider and narrower spacing, keeping the structure low. Compare designs against the same two goals: staying up and leaving room.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Draw the design that worked for your toy and name one improvement you made.

personalPrompt: When have you made or fixed something to fit a particular need? Share what you checked before calling it finished.
careNote: Build on the floor with large lightweight parts and a low roof. This shelter is only for a toy; no climbing, standing on structures, staples, or sharp cardboard edges.

title: Fold a standing picture
subtitle: Help a paper character stand on its own.
takeaway: Folds and a wider base can help a lightweight paper model stand.
parentPrimer: A flat sheet often needs support to stay upright. Try a folded base or a tent fold and compare how the paper stands on a level surface. There are several workable designs. Keep the goal small: a picture that stands for a moment without a hand holding it.
materials: Several large sheets of paper or thin card

toddler.action: Decorate a large sheet, help press an adult-started fold, or choose where the picture stands.
toddler.question: Shall our picture stand here?

older.action: Try two folds, compare their bases, and adapt one so the picture stands more steadily.
older.question: What part touches the table and holds our picture up?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Draw a simple face on paper and wonder how it could stand to greet you.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Try the flat sheet, then add a broad fold at its bottom. Notice what now touches the table.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Let your younger son decorate while your older son tries a base fold and a tent fold with help. Stand the pictures on a level table and adjust them after a wobble. Arrange a small gallery and give each character a name.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Choose a favourite standing picture and remember the fold that helped it balance.

personalPrompt: Where have you used a fold, brace, or support to solve a practical problem? Show it with the paper.
careNote: Use large sheets with smooth edges. An adult starts firm folds; avoid sharp creases near faces and collect torn scraps. No scissors, staples, or clips are needed.

title: A sign for our space
subtitle: Make a useful message with a picture and a few words.
takeaway: We can design a sign around the person who needs to understand it.
parentPrimer: Choose a real small purpose, such as showing where books belong. Draw a clear picture and add a short label. Ask someone who did not design it what they think it means, then improve it if needed. A sign is useful when its audience can understand it, even if they cannot read the words.
materials: A large sheet of paper or card
A shelf or low table where the sign can rest

toddler.action: Choose a picture or colour and point to the place the sign is for.
toddler.question: What picture could help us find the books?

older.action: Plan a picture and short label, test the message with a family member, and revise one detail.
older.question: Would someone who cannot read the words know what this means?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Look for a familiar place that could use a friendly sign.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Sketch two possible pictures and talk about which tells the message more clearly.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can choose or draw a feature while your older son adds a label with your help. Ask a family member what the sign suggests, without giving the answer first. Change a confusing detail and place the sign on a low surface.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Use the sign together and remember a choice that made it easier to understand.

personalPrompt: What sign, label, or diagram has helped you do something? Share what made it clear.
careNote: Use chunky crayons and large card without clips or pins. Rest the sign securely on a low surface; do not place it on safety signs, controls, doorways, or climbing spots.

title: One small patch of nature
subtitle: Look closely at a place you usually pass.
takeaway: Looking slowly at a small place can reveal details we missed at first.
parentPrimer: Choose a safe patch visible from a path or window, such as the base of a tree. Observe without collecting or disturbing anything. Notice shapes, colours, and movement rather than trying to identify every species. A drawing can record what was actually there and leave unknown details as questions.
materials: A safe view of a small outdoor patch

toddler.action: Point to a colour, shape, or movement and make a mark for it beside you.
toddler.question: What can you show me in our little patch?

older.action: Look again for a detail missed the first time and add it to a drawing with a question.
older.question: What did you notice after we slowed down?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Choose a small outdoor patch to explore with your eyes from a safe place.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Name one visible detail and model saying you are unsure about something else.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Take short looking breaks, then draw. Your younger son can point or choose a colour while your older son records shapes and movement. Look at the same patch again and add a newly noticed detail without collecting anything.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Date the shared picture and choose something to look for on a future visit.

personalPrompt: Which ordinary outdoor place have you come to know well? Tell them a small detail you enjoy noticing there.
careNote: An adult chooses and supervises a safe viewing place away from roads, water, and unknown plants or animal waste. Stay on paths, leave wildlife undisturbed, and keep windows safely secured.

title: What the wind moves
subtitle: Find clues to a breeze without chasing it.
takeaway: Moving leaves and branches can give us clues about the wind.
parentPrimer: Observe a familiar tree or shrub from a safe sheltered position or window. Look for movement rather than making an exact wind measurement. If nothing moves, that is an observation too. Compare brief moments and distinguish what you see from a guess about how the air feels outside.
materials: A safe view of a tree or shrub

toddler.action: Point to moving leaves or copy a gentle swaying motion with a hand.
toddler.question: Can you see anything moving?

older.action: Draw arrows or marks for movement and compare two short observations of the same view.
older.question: What clue makes you think there is a breeze?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Look at the same branch together and wait briefly to see whether it moves.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Describe only what you can see, then explain why moving leaves might be a clue about wind.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Watch in short comfortable pauses. Your younger son can point or move a hand while your older son draws movement marks. Compare a second observation after drawing, and record calm moments as well as moving ones.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Keep one observation about the wind and one question about the outdoor view.

personalPrompt: When has the wind changed your plans or caught your attention? Share a small everyday memory.
careNote: Observe from a secure window or a safe sheltered place in mild weather. Avoid storms, damaged branches, roads, and climbing to see better; do not attach strings or ribbons to children.

title: Colours through the window
subtitle: Make a palette of a familiar outdoor view.
takeaway: A familiar outdoor place can contain many colours and change over time.
parentPrimer: Choose a view and match a few visible colours with crayons. Describe where each appears rather than making assumptions about the season. A leaf may show several colours, and lighting can change how something looks. Date the page so it can become a record for a later comparison.
materials: A safe outdoor view from a secure window or path

toddler.action: Choose a crayon for something they notice and make a patch of colour.
toddler.question: Which colour would you like to use for that?

older.action: Make a small colour key with labels or drawings showing where each colour appeared.
older.question: Can you find two different colours on the same plant?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Pick one colour in the view and invite everyone to find where it appears.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Make a colour patch on paper and add a small drawing showing its source.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can choose colours while your older son builds a key. Look for several colours in one object and similar colours in different places. Draw a shared view without requiring an exact colour match.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Date the page and choose a place in the view you might compare on another day.

personalPrompt: What colours remind you of a favourite outdoor place or time of year? Share that memory without expecting today's view to match.
careNote: Keep windows secured and children off windowsills. Outdoors, stay with an adult on a safe path and observe unknown plants without touching or tasting them.

title: A place for everyone
subtitle: Plan a table that people can use comfortably.
takeaway: Preparing a shared meal includes thinking about what each person needs.
parentPrimer: Use empty lightweight cups, plates, and spoons to plan a simple table. Check how many places you need and whether each item is easy to reach. Different arrangements may work. This is a chance to practise preparation and consideration without handling hot food or sharp utensils.
materials: Lightweight unbreakable plates and empty cups

toddler.action: Carry one lightweight item with you and choose where a napkin belongs.
toddler.question: Who needs a cup here?

older.action: Plan a place for each person, check the items, and adjust anything difficult to reach.
older.question: How can we tell that everyone has what they need?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Imagine a small family meal and count who will join it.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Arrange one place and explain why a cup and spoon should be easy to reach.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Let your younger son deliver napkins while your older son checks each place. Sit or stand comfortably to try the arrangement, move an awkward item, and practise clearing it together. Repeat with a pretend extra guest if wanted.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Choose one helpful preparation job to remember for a future meal.

personalPrompt: What small preparation makes meals calmer in your home? Share a routine the children can help with.
careNote: Use empty unbreakable dishes and large spoons on a stable low surface. Keep knives, hot food, glass, and trailing tablecloths out of the activity.

title: Spread, smooth, and swirl
subtitle: Practise a small kitchen skill with a familiar snack.
takeaway: A gentle tool movement can spread a soft ingredient across a surface.
parentPrimer: Choose a familiar soft food and spread that the parent already prepares safely for both children. Demonstrate a small amount and a slow movement with the back of a spoon. Explore broad strokes and little swirls. The goal is participating in preparation, not producing a tidy result or eating a set amount.
materials: A familiar soft snack base prepared appropriately by an adult
A familiar smooth spread suitable for both children

toddler.action: Guide a spoon with your help, choose where to start, or watch and describe the movement.
toddler.question: Shall we make a little swirl here?

older.action: Try two gentle spreading movements and decide which covers the surface more easily.
older.question: What changes when you use less spread or a lighter touch?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Wash hands together and look at the soft ingredient on a spoon.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Show a small amount spreading slowly with the back of the spoon. Keep each person's portion separate.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can guide a spoon with you while your older son experiments with broad strokes and small swirls. Compare the movements, prepare a small snack if wanted, and help wipe the work area. Include pauses and watching.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Remember a movement that helped and thank each person for a preparation or cleanup job.

personalPrompt: Who showed you a useful kitchen technique? Share a small tip that makes this task easier.
careNote: The adult chooses familiar foods suitable for each child's allergies and eating needs and prepares all portions. Use no knives or hot ingredients. Supervise continuously, keep children seated for any eating, and never require tasting.

title: Keep a recipe in pictures
subtitle: Turn a familiar cold snack into a guide for next time.
takeaway: A recipe can record ingredients and an order so we can make something again.
parentPrimer: Choose a familiar simple cold snack the parent already prepares safely, such as plain yoghurt with a suitable familiar topping. Draw the ingredients and two or three steps before preparing it together. After trying the guide, add a missing detail. This is documenting your own routine rather than following a new dietary recipe.
materials: Parent-selected familiar ingredients for a simple cold snack

toddler.action: Point to an ingredient picture, help with a spoon, or mark a step as finished.
toddler.question: Which picture shows what comes next?

older.action: Draw the ingredient list and steps, follow the guide with you, and add a detail that would help next time.
older.question: What might someone need to know that our picture has not shown yet?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Choose a familiar cold snack and wash hands before handling its ingredients.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Sketch the ingredients and the first preparation step. Explain how the pictures can help you remember.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can point to pictures while your older son adds the remaining steps. The adult handles all ingredient preparation, then supports spooning or mixing. Follow the guide, notice a missing detail, and add it before cleaning up together.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Give the recipe a family title and keep the picture guide for another day. Eating is optional.

personalPrompt: Is there a family snack or recipe you know by heart? Share how you learned it and what you would write down for someone else.
careNote: The adult checks allergies and individual eating needs, prepares suitable portions, and supervises continuously. Use no raw animal products, heat, sharp tools, or small hard toppings. Any eating happens seated without pressure to taste.

title: Fast, slow, same pattern
subtitle: Change the pace of a gentle tapping pattern.
takeaway: We can perform the same rhythm at different speeds.
parentPrimer: Choose a short pattern such as tap, tap, pause. Keep its order and relative spacing while changing the overall pace. Tempo is the speed; rhythm is the arrangement of sounds and silences. Start slowly enough for everyone to join and use quiet taps or visible hand movements.
materials: A cushion or your knees for gentle tapping

toddler.action: Join with one quiet tap, watch your hands, or choose whether the next round is slower.
toddler.question: Shall our taps go slowly?

older.action: Keep a short pattern recognisable while changing its pace, then explain what stayed the same.
older.question: Did our pattern change, or just how quickly we played it?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Play a quiet tap-tap-pause pattern and invite anyone to join.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Repeat it more slowly, stretching the spaces too. Name the difference between the pattern and its pace.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can choose a comfortable pace while your older son leads the pattern. Draw two dots and a space as a reminder. Alternate short rounds with rests, and try silent hand movements as another way to join.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Perform a favourite comfortable version and remember which part stayed the same.

personalPrompt: When does the pace of music change how an activity feels for you? Share an example while keeping the tapping gentle.
careNote: Keep taps quiet and comfortable, avoid hard surfaces or striking objects near ears, and let children watch or use silent movements. No fast pace is required.

title: The quiet conductor
subtitle: Use a gesture to bring sounds in and let them rest.
takeaway: Shared signals can help a group start, stop, and make music together.
parentPrimer: Agree on two signals, such as open hands for a gentle sound and resting hands for silence. A conductor helps people coordinate; the game is cooperation rather than obedience. Keep sounds quiet and let the leader wait until everyone is ready. Silent motions can replace sound throughout.

toddler.action: Choose a gentle sound or show a start signal while an adult helps the group follow.
toddler.question: Shall our little band play or rest?

older.action: Lead a short sequence of sound and silence, using clear signals and watching the group's readiness.
older.question: How can your hands make the next change clear?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Make one quiet sound together and let it come to a rest.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Agree on start and rest gestures, then model a very short round with a generous pause.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Take turns conducting. Your younger son can give one signal while your older son plans a short sequence with silence. Try taps, hums, or silent hand openings, letting anyone change their choice or sit out.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Finish with a shared quiet pause and name one gesture that helped you play together.

personalPrompt: When have you followed or given a helpful cue in a group? Share how people knew what was coming next.
careNote: Keep all sounds at a comfortable volume and avoid startling starts. Do not use whistles, sticks, or loud instruments; watching quietly is welcome.

title: Draw a little score
subtitle: Make picture instructions for a tiny piece of music.
takeaway: Marks on a page can remind us which sounds and silences to make.
parentPrimer: Invent a few shared marks: a dot for a quiet tap, a wavy line for a hum, and a blank box for silence. Agree on their meanings and read three boxes from left to right. This is an invented graphic score, so it does not need to match conventional music notation.
materials: A large sheet of paper divided into three boxes

toddler.action: Choose a mark or make a quiet sound for one box, with an adult following their lead.
toddler.question: What sound shall this picture ask for?

older.action: Make a simple key, compose three boxes, and check whether someone can perform the score using it.
older.question: How will another person know what this mark means?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Draw a dot and give it a quiet tap as its sound.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Choose another mark and a silent box. Show how the key explains what each means.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can choose one box while your older son arranges the whole score. Point along the boxes as you perform it. Swap one mark, play the revised version, and let a new leader follow the key.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Name the little piece and keep its score with the key beside it.

personalPrompt: What reminders help you follow or remember a piece of music? Share a way of recording an idea before it disappears.
careNote: Use chunky crayons and quiet sounds, with silent gestures as an option. Keep paper free of clips and do not tap hard objects or surfaces near anyone's ears.

title: The other character's story
subtitle: Tell the same small event from two viewpoints.
takeaway: Different characters can notice different parts of the same event.
parentPrimer: Invent a small event with two large toys, such as arriving at a pretend picnic. Tell it first from one toy's viewpoint, then the other's. Keep the main event consistent while changing what each notices or wants. These are imagined possibilities, not claims about how real people must feel.

toddler.action: Choose a toy, give it a sound, or show where it goes in the story.
toddler.question: What does your toy notice?

older.action: Retell the event as each toy and explain which details or wishes changed with the viewpoint.
older.question: What might this character notice that the other one missed?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Let two toys arrive at the same pretend picnic.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Tell one short version as the first toy, then another as its companion.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can move a character while your older son gives each a viewpoint. Keep the setting and main event the same, but try different things each toy notices. Draw two pictures of the shared moment and dictate their words.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Remember one detail the characters shared and one they described differently.

personalPrompt: Have two people remembered different details of a shared day? Tell a gentle example without deciding that one person's feelings were wrong.
careNote: Use large soft toys without detachable parts. Keep the invented event reassuring and let children choose whether to speak for a character or simply move it.

title: Choose another ending
subtitle: Give one story two possible ways forward.
takeaway: A character's choice can send a story towards a different ending.
parentPrimer: Invent a small problem, such as a toy finding a closed pretend shop. Offer two choices that both fit the beginning: return later or make a pretend shop at home. Explore each without declaring one the correct ending. Keep track of which events belong to which version.

toddler.action: Choose a picture for what happens next or act out a simple move with the toy.
toddler.question: Shall our toy go home or wait with a friend?

older.action: Invent two choices and show how each leads to a different ending while keeping the beginning the same.
older.question: What changed in our ending because of that choice?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Start a story about a toy whose pretend shop is closed.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Draw the shared beginning in one panel and suggest two possible next steps.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can choose which path to act out first while your older son builds its ending. Return to the same beginning and try the other choice. Draw the endings in the remaining panels and compare how each followed from a choice.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Give both versions a title and choose an ending to retell, without needing to rank them.

personalPrompt: When has a small change of plan led to an unexpected experience? Share a family-friendly example that could inspire a story.
careNote: Use large toys and chunky crayons. Keep the imaginary problem small and reassuring, and change the story if either child finds it upsetting.

title: A postcard from somewhere imaginary
subtitle: Invent a place and send a pretend message home.
takeaway: Specific details help someone imagine a place they have never visited.
parentPrimer: Invent a gentle imaginary place, such as a town of enormous cushions. Choose a few details about what a visitor sees, hears, and does. Draw a postcard and dictate a short message. Keep a distinction between real memories and invented details while welcoming either as inspiration.
materials: A large sheet of paper folded like a postcard

toddler.action: Choose a colour or feature for the place and move the toy through the imagined scene.
toddler.question: What can our visitor see here?

older.action: Invent a place with two or three connected details, then dictate or write a message about one event there.
older.question: Which detail would help someone picture our place?

steps.title: Spark a little curiosity
steps.instruction: Let a toy announce a visit to a place that does not exist yet.

steps.title: Share what you know
steps.instruction: Invent a name and one concrete detail, then show how you might draw it on a postcard.

steps.title: Make a discovery together
steps.instruction: Your younger son can add a feature while your older son connects it to a little event. Guide the toy through the scene, draw the postcard, and record a short message for a pretend recipient. Add a detail after hearing the message aloud.

steps.title: Keep a little memory
steps.instruction: Read or show the postcard together and remember which parts you invented.

personalPrompt: What detail do you remember most clearly from somewhere you visited? Use it as a starting point for an invented place.
careNote: Use large paper and chunky crayons without stamps, stickers, or clips that could become small loose parts. Keep the imaginary journey comfortable and let children change any detail.
